0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4.title: Objects of Exchange and Mobility
0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4.quote: Exchange had long been part of travel along the Hajj route, as pilgrims carried goods to trade and help sustain their journey. The movement of objects, textiles, and currencies reveals enduring networks of exchange, while commemorative items reflect the profound impact and growing significance of the railway.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317.title: Building the Sultan’s Dream
0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317.quote: The Hijaz Railway was more than a simple infrastructure project; beneath its promise of connection and pilgrimage lay a political and military agenda, reinforcing Ottoman authority and projecting imperial control across the territories it traversed.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50.title: The Train Station That Once Was, but Is No More
2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50.quote: Can an infrastructure that has ceased to function continue to operate as a metaphor?

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532.title: By Rail, by Road and by Sky
47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532.quote: The post-war landscape of the region required new methods of interconnections and infrastructures of travel. Train travel declined due to the rise of the automobile and airplane. These technologies, however, were only possible due to the extraction of oil which itself transformed the area.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d.title: Modernity Meets Timelessness
47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d.quote: The Hijaz Railway became a powerful symbol of Ottoman modernity, carrying steel, machinery and new technologies across the desert. As the tracks cut through the Hijazi landscape, they introduced a striking modern infrastructure into an ancient environment.

705dfb0c-00cf-54a9-9f9d-314ae8771258.title: Lines of History
705dfb0c-00cf-54a9-9f9d-314ae8771258.presentation: The Hijaz Railway was one of the most ambitious projects of the late Ottoman Empire. Launched under Sultan Abdülhamid II in 1900, it connected Damascus to Medina and reshaped the relationship between pilgrimage, politics, technology, and landscape. By tracing its historical development, this theme presents the railway not only as an infrastructure project, but also as a symbol of Ottoman modernity and Pan-Islamic unity. Through maps, photographs, postcards, medals, architectural remains, and archival documents, it explores how the railway strengthened imperial authority, facilitated the Hajj, transformed cities and stations, and introduced modern technologies into the desert.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8.title: Travellers and Identities
70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8.quote: Pilgrims, merchants, soldiers, diplomats and other travellers brought different languages, beliefs, and traditions to the Hijaz Railway. Their journeys reveal a world of identities shaped by religion, culture, and community, reflecting growing international interest in the region.

7233ff48-d3bc-569e-a2a1-51267d0afd15.title: Vision and Contemporary Reflections
7233ff48-d3bc-569e-a2a1-51267d0afd15.presentation:
When the Ottoman Empire collapsed at the end of the First World War, the Hijaz Railway lost the political order that had given it meaning. New states and Mandates emerged, national movements carried hopes of independence, and new borders cut across a line built from Damascus to Medina.  
In the decades that followed, oil extraction transformed the region's landscapes, cities and economies, while roads and air routes redefined how people, pilgrims and goods moved.  
But the railway did not simply disappear. For poets and artists across the region, the train became an image of exile, migration, labour and the wish to return home, reflecting the realities of displacement and loss that still mark the region today.  
More recently, regional plans to reconnect Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria and Türkiye by rail have revived the possibility of trains returning to this corridor.  
This theme follows the railway's afterlife across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries and asks a simple but persistent question. Can an infrastructure that has ceased to function continue to operate as a metaphor for freedom of movement?

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5.title: Architecture as an Agent of Change
744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5.quote: The Hijaz Railway reshaped the urban and architectural landscapes it crossed. From fortress-like stations in the desert to more modern structures in major cities, it adapted to local conditions while transforming the fabric of the places it connected.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666.title: Territories of Encounter
9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666.quote: The railway connected vibrant and diverse cultures and territories. Stations became new points of encounter in landscapes already shaped by bazaars, hammams, mosques, tekkiyas and other monuments. These cultures shaped the identities and memories of people who lived in and travelled through these places.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4.title: Along the line, through the window
a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4.quote: Travelling the Hijaz Railway would have been a physical and emotional experience. In crowded carriages travellers moved through cities, past mountains, wadis and deserts. They crossed bridges and observed stations and monuments. Remarkably varied landscapes could be encountered along the journey.

cb53097b-7a56-5261-8740-2063238f1dc7.title: About
cb53097b-7a56-5261-8740-2063238f1dc7.presentation:
The Hijaz Railway is part of a shared history that connects people and places across today’s borders. Construction began in 1900 under Sultan Abdulhamid II, and by 1908 the railway connected Damascus to Medina. Conceived in the late Ottoman Empire for religious, political, strategic and economic reasons, it facilitated the journey of pilgrims towards the Hijaz while linking communities across vast territories. The railway carried passengers, goods and ideas, creating both a physical and symbolic connection across a region of multiple identities.  
  
Local and international conflicts during the First World War transformed the region and the territories through which the railway passed. Sections were damaged or abandoned, while new political borders divided a landscape once connected by rail. Yet traces of the rail line remained: in stations and monuments, objects and photographs, and in the collective memories of communities along its route.  
  
*The Hijaz Railway: Memories and Visions* expounds on this legacy through material culture. The exhibition examines the railway’s impact on people, cities and landscapes, and the ways in which its history continues to resonate across the diverse regions it once connected.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5.title: Engineering Sacred Mobility
d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5.quote: The Hijaz Railway transformed the journey itself, making travel shorter, safer and more accessible. By reducing the hardships of long-distance movement and pilgrimage, it opened the route to a wider range of travellers and reshaped the experience of mobility across the Hijaz.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559.title: New Beginnings and Hopes
e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559.quote: After the First World War, new opportunities and challenges became evident in the changing region. As new states and Mandates emerged, their borders cut across the path of the Hijaz Railway.

f9fbfb04-4e15-5b34-8b72-548b41e013c8.title: From the Train Window
f9fbfb04-4e15-5b34-8b72-548b41e013c8.presentation:
The Hijaz Railway transformed movement along a centuries-old pilgrimage corridor connecting Damascus to the Hijaz. Built primarily to facilitate the Hajj, it also served the wider ambitions of the Ottoman Empire. A powerful symbol of modernity and technological progress, the railway reduced a journey of several weeks to only a few days, saving pilgrims time and money. It emerged at a time of profound social and political transformation in a region on the verge of dramatic change.  
Pilgrims, merchants, soldiers, workers and other diverse passengers travelled with goods, objects and ideas. Stations became meeting places, linking cities, agricultural communities, pilgrimage sites, desert forts and tribal territories. Travellers encountered shifting landscapes and a mosaic of peoples, identities and traditions.  
Long before the railway was built, pilgrimage, trade and travel had brought people together along this route. The railway transformed their experiences of cultural diversity and their shared heritage.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/d4a.contextual_description: This portrait of Sultan Abdülhamid II, the principal patron of the Hijaz Railway, evokes the political and religious ambitions behind the project. The railway reinforced Ottoman authority across the empire while supporting the Sultan’s wider pan-Islamic policy. Paired with the portrait of the Sharif of Mecca, it reflects the interaction between Ottoman imperial power and religious authority in the Hijaz.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/47e.contextual_description: This lithographed postcard portrays the Sharif of Mecca, representing the local political and religious authority of the Hijaz. His position complements that of Sultan Abdülhamid II, illustrating the different layers of authority surrounding Ottoman rule, pilgrimage, and the Holy Cities.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/e7c.contextual_description: The blueprint reflects the political ambitions behind the Hijaz Railway. Its planned continuation from Medina to Mecca reveals the project’s wider imperial vision, while Meissner Pasha’s signature points to Ottoman-German technical cooperation. The marked tribal territories highlight the complex political landscape crossed by the railway. Dated June 1916, at the outbreak of the Arab Revolt, the map captures a moment when Ottoman authority in the region was being directly challenged.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/6ce.contextual_description: The telegraph connection between Damascus and the Hijaz prefigured the Hijaz Railway and formed part of the same wider Ottoman vision of integrating and controlling distant provinces through modern infrastructure. Erected prominently in Marjeh Square, the memorial column transformed this technological achievement into a public symbol of imperial authority and administration. Its political significance was reinforced by its architect, Raimondo D’Aronco, who served Sultan Abdülhamid II and worked closely within the imperial court.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/40c.contextual_description: By situating the Hijaz Railway within the administrative geography of the Vilayet of Syria, the map reveals its role as an instrument of Ottoman territorial control. The railway strengthened communication, administration and troop movement across a politically sensitive region, helping consolidate imperial authority over Syria, Transjordan and the northern Hijaz.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/29b.contextual_description: Issued under Sultan Abdülhamid II, the medal transformed financial contribution into symbolic loyalty, visually and materially linking donors to the Sultan through the tuğra and the locomotive, and honorific titles such as “bey“ and “pasha“. By framing the railway as a project “built by Muslims, for Muslims,” the medal promoted the Ottoman Empire as protector and leader of the Muslim Umma, reinforcing Abdülhamid II’s pan-Islamic agenda. Together with the related items it illustrates how the railway’s funding, construction and public representation were closely intertwined with loyalty to the Sultan and the Empire.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/a16.contextual_description: This medal commemorated the inauguration of Maʿan Station and was awarded to major donors who helped finance the Hijaz Railway. It turned financial support into public recognition, linking the expansion of the line with loyalty to the Sultan and presenting the railway as a collective Muslim project under Ottoman leadership.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/ab3.contextual_description: This rail section bears a commemorative inscription naming Sultan Abdülhamid II as Amir al-Mu’minin and Ghazi. By inscribing the Sultan’s titles directly onto the railway material, the object linked the physical construction of the line with imperial authority, religious legitimacy, and public commemoration.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/f2e.contextual_description: This section of track from Medina Station is engraved with the year 1908, marking the opening of the station and the arrival of the first train from Istanbul. The inscription turns the railway itself into a commemorative object, celebrating the completion of the line to Medina as an imperial achievement.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/a9d.contextual_description: This silver pocket watch combines the image of a Hijaz Railway locomotive with the Ottoman coat of arms. Likely produced for an official connected with the railway’s construction, it shows how the project entered commemorative and personal objects, turning participation in the railway into a visible sign of imperial service and prestige.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/d14.contextual_description: This imperial decree presents Sultan Abdülhamid II as the first contributor to the Hijaz Railway, donating one month of his salary and calling on ministers, officials, and Muslims more broadly to support the project. It turned fundraising into a public expression of loyalty, piety, and collective responsibility.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/c29.contextual_description: This table records the revenues and expenditures of the Hamidiye Hijaz Railway up to July 1902. It reveals the administrative and financial organisation behind the project, showing how contributions and expenses were systematically documented as the Ottoman state managed the railway’s construction.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/102.contextual_description: This bridge inscription transformed railway infrastructure into a visible statement of Ottoman authority. By marking a structure built along the Hamidiye Hijaz Railway, it linked engineering works with imperial patronage and made the railway itself a medium through which the state projected power and presence.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/4dc.contextual_description: This list records donors considered eligible to receive nickel medals for supporting the construction of the Hamidiye Hijaz Railway. The inclusion of contributors from Punjab and other parts of India shows how fundraising extended beyond the Ottoman Empire, turning donations into a transregional expression of Muslim solidarity and loyalty.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/dd7.contextual_description: This 1912 statistical report records the Hijaz Railway’s income, expenditure, passenger and freight traffic, train movements, kilometres travelled, and capital. It shows the railway as a fully operating system, managed through detailed financial and administrative monitoring.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/8c3.contextual_description: This gold medal honours those who rendered service and support to the Hamidiye Hejaz Railway, as stated in its reverse inscription. The obverse displays Sultan Abdülhamid II’s tuğra and the title “El Gazi” above a locomotive, enclosed within a wreath. These elements associate contributions to the railway with imperial recognition, linking modern infrastructure to the Sultan’s authority. Alongside the silver medal, this gold example transforms the participation into a tangible expression of loyalty to the Sultan and his pan-Islamic vision.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/145.contextual_description: Issued under Sultan Abdülhamid II, this gold medal commemorates the official opening of the Maʿan section of the Hamidiye Hejaz Railway in 1322 AH / 1904. Its obverse combines the Sultan’s tuğra and the title “el-Gazi” with a locomotive, associating imperial authority with technological progress. The reverse inscription records the inauguration, presenting the railway’s expansion as an achievement of the Sultan’s reign. Together with the silver medal recognising financial contributions, it illustrates how Ottoman commemorative medals linked the railway’s funding and construction to imperial patronage and loyalty.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/d02.contextual_description: The postcard presents Haifa Station as an imperial asset, framed by Ottoman stamps and crowned with the imperial coat of arms, clearly asserting Ottoman sovereignty over the railway and the wider region of Bilad al-Sham. Its production by the German printer Ottmar Zieher also reflects the broader Ottoman–German networks that accompanied the railway’s development. Seen alongside the earlier Jaffa–Jerusalem railway and its station at Jaffa, Haifa formed part of a wider expansion of modern railway infrastructure in Ottoman Palestine, shaped by both imperial ambitions and foreign technical involvement.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/b25.contextual_description: Although Jaffa Station was not part of the Hijaz Railway, it offers an important comparison with Haifa. Opened in 1892 on the French-built Jaffa–Jerusalem line, it formed part of the wider railway modernisation of Ottoman Palestine. Like Haifa, its representation also helped turn railway infrastructure into an image of progress, connectivity, and political presence.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/87b.contextual_description: These official Hijaz Railway postcards combined fundraising with propaganda. Sold through local post offices, they depicted construction works, general views, and inauguration ceremonies, transforming the railway into a widely circulated image of Ottoman modernity and achievement. Their German production also reflects the international networks surrounding the project.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/8fb.contextual_description: This view of Mecca by Austrian orientalist Andreas Magnus Hunglinger offers an earlier European representation of the region, before the visual language of railway modernity. In contrast with the Haifa postcard, it shows how representations of Bilad al-Sham and the Hijaz shifted from picturesque views toward images of infrastructure, progress, and imperial power.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/59a.contextual_description: Bakırköy Railway Station represents the wider expansion of the Ottoman railway network during the nineteenth century and the imperial policies that later shaped the Hijaz Railway. Together with the related items, it shows how railways became more than transport infrastructure. They supported administration, military mobility, political representation, and the projection of Ottoman authority across distant provinces.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/9b5.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway delegations reflect the political and administrative mobilisation behind the project. They show how the railway was promoted as an instrument for integrating distant Ottoman provinces, strengthening imperial authority, facilitating military movement, and connecting the capital with the Hijaz.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/e9a.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway delegations reflect the political and administrative mobilisation behind the project. They show how the railway was promoted as an instrument for integrating distant Ottoman provinces, strengthening imperial authority, facilitating military movement, and connecting the capital with the Hijaz.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/141.contextual_description: This German field-postcard shows a wartime procession outside Damascus’s Hijaz Railway Station after the arrival of Jamal Pasha. With military bands, cadets, and youth corps gathered around the station, it presents railway architecture as a stage for ceremony, mobilisation, and the public display of Ottoman military authority across all its controlled lands.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/b2e.contextual_description: This image records the foundation-laying ceremony for the new station and workshop at Daraa, attended by senior Ottoman officials. It shows railway construction as a public and political event, linking the physical expansion of the Hijaz Railway with state administration, imperial representation, and official ceremony.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/d06.contextual_description: This image shows an Ottoman military camp at Medina, accompanied by Urdu poetry praising Turkish soldiers as defenders of Islam, the Prophet, and the Holy Cities. Produced in Delhi for an Indian Muslim audience, it reflects how Ottoman authority in the Hijaz was celebrated beyond the empire as protection of pilgrimage and the Muslim community.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/62c.contextual_description: This German military propaganda postcard reflects the Ottoman–German alliance in Bilad al-Sham during the First World War, linking military cooperation with infrastructure such as the Hijaz Railway. The railway functioned not only as a transport system, but as a strategic asset for communication, troop movement, and imperial control. Read together with the related British archival files, the item also reveals how German influence and the railway’s political and military role were closely monitored by rival European powers.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/1f3.contextual_description: This British archival file documents how the Hijaz Railway was closely monitored by rival European powers. Reports on its route, construction, German engineers, and foreign influence reveal British concern over the railway’s strategic importance and the wider political implications of Ottoman–German cooperation.

0e141b33-0d0b-5751-95ed-4573ce900317/8da.contextual_description: The painting’s composition brings political authority and sacred geography into a single visual field. Commemorating the 1909 pilgrimage of Abbas Hilmi II, Khedive of Egypt, it places his portrait opposite that of Sultan Mehmed V Rashad, around the Kaʿbah, the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina and the Dome of the Rock. This arrangement reflects the close relationship between Ottoman political legitimacy and guardianship of Islam’s holy places. The Hijaz Railway, which had reached Medina only a year earlier, formed part of this same strategy: strengthening access to the pilgrimage while reinforcing Ottoman authority and its claim to leadership within the wider Muslim world.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/182.contextual_description: This map situates the Hajj within the wider geography of travel, trade and pilgrimage before the Hijaz Railway. The caravan and pilgrim routes linking North Africa, the Mediterranean, Egypt, Syria, the Red Sea and Mecca reveal a journey made through multiple interconnected land and sea networks. Pilgrims travelled across vast distances, often through difficult and fragmented routes. In this context, the Hijaz Railway marked a major transformation, shortening the journey, improving accessibility and creating a more direct connection toward the Holy Cities.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/1a9.contextual_description: This map shows the Hijaz Railway completed from Damascus to Medina, with projected extensions toward Mecca. In contrast with the older caravan routes of the main item, it presents pilgrimage travel as a more direct, structured, and modern system, illustrating the transformation introduced by the railway.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/c57.contextual_description: Anis al-Hujjaj evokes the experience of the Hajj before the arrival of modern railway travel. Written during the author’s pilgrimage from India to Mecca in 1676–77, it records the length, complexity, dangers and practical organisation of the journey. Its illustrations show ships crossing hazardous seas, pilgrims camping under the harsh desert sun, armed escorts providing protection and the careful organisation of food, shelter and movement. The manuscript also captures the social diversity of the Hajj, bringing together travellers from different regions and backgrounds.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/dc7.contextual_description: This written account of The March of the Caravan from Cairo to Mecca documents the scale, organisation and hardships of the Hajj from Cairo before the Hijaz Railway. The journey required animals, supplies, military protection and careful logistical preparation across long desert routes, making pilgrimage both physically demanding and time-consuming. The later railway transformed this experience by shortening travel times, reducing many of the dangers and difficulties of the route and making access to the Holy Cities faster, safer and more accessible to a broader range of pilgrims.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/48a.contextual_description: This coloured print presents a bird’s-eye view of Mecca, with the Holy Mosque and the Kaʿbah at its centre, surrounded by pilgrims approaching the city across the desert. The image emphasises the scale, endurance, and collective nature of the Hajj, while also highlighting a limitation that remained after the construction of the Hijaz Railway. Although the railway made the journey to Medina significantly faster and safer, it never reached Mecca. Pilgrims therefore still had to complete the final stage of the pilgrimage overland, preserving an older pattern of travel even within the new railway era. The image thus captures both continuity and transformation in the experience of reaching the Holy City.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/7fc.contextual_description: This panorama extends the story of the pilgrimage beyond arrival in Mecca, showing pilgrims gathered at Mina during the celebrations of the Hajj. It highlights the collective and ritual dimension of the journey, reminding us that reaching the Holy City was only one stage within a longer sequence of sacred movements and ceremonies.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/7e3.contextual_description: The Mahmal was one of the most visible ceremonial and political symbols of the Hajj. Carried with the official pilgrim caravans from Cairo and Damascus, it represented not only devotion but also the authority of the rulers who claimed responsibility for protecting the Holy Cities. Under Ottoman rule, it became closely associated with the Sultan’s political and religious presence in the Hijaz. Seen alongside the Hijaz Railway, the Mahmal shows how an older tradition of pilgrimage, ceremony and imperial legitimacy was incorporated into a new age of modern transport.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/32b.contextual_description: This image shows the departure of the Cairo Hajj caravan from Bab al-Nasr, with the Mahmal forming part of a carefully organised procession of officials, guards, merchants, supplies and pilgrims. It highlights the ceremonial and logistical complexity of the pre-rail pilgrimage, before the Hijaz Railway transformed long-distance travel.

Carried with the official pilgrim caravans from Cairo and Damascus, it represented not only devotion but also the authority of the rulers who claimed responsibility for protecting the Holy Cities. d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/4d5.contextual_description:
This photograph shows a railway station 74 km north of Medina, demonstrating how infrastructure brought the Holy City closer to pilgrims. It represents how the railway made travel safer and more organized for Hajj pilgrims, reducing the need to rely on long and risky caravan routes.  
By documenting a station in the Hijaz, the photograph embodies the social impact of the railway by creating physical and institutional support for pilgrims during their journey.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/99d.contextual_description: This image shows a group of pilgrims gathered beside a train, capturing how the Hijaz Railway transformed the experience of pilgrimage. By reducing travel time and easing the difficulties of long-distance journeys, the railway made access to the Holy Cities faster and more accessible to larger numbers of pilgrims. The juxtaposition of the travellers and the train reflects a new era of mobility, in which modern transport reshaped one of the oldest pilgrimage routes in the Islamic world.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/42d.contextual_description: This image shows a group of pilgrims gathered beside a train, capturing how the Hijaz Railway transformed the experience of pilgrimage. By reducing travel time and easing the difficulties of long-distance journeys, the railway made access to the Holy Cities faster and more accessible to larger numbers of pilgrims. The juxtaposition of the travellers and the train reflects a new era of mobility, in which modern transport reshaped one of the oldest pilgrimage routes in the Islamic world.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/a6d.contextual_description: This photocard shows adults and children with provisions waiting for a train, while heavily loaded camels stand nearby. The mix of ages suggests how railway travel opened long-distance movement to a broader range of travellers, while the continued presence of camels shows that older forms of transport remained essential beyond the stations.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/c76.contextual_description: This view of Medina Station shows pilgrims waiting beside the railway at the northern end of the Hajj rail journey. Similar to the main item, it captures people gathered around the train, but here the setting is especially significant: Medina marked the railway’s terminus, after which pilgrims continuing to Mecca had to resume their journey by other means.

d8a5bd81-c1f8-52db-a349-bb93b84539a5/345.contextual_description: Published in 1889, Bilder aus Mekka offers one of the earliest photographic records of the Hajj, documenting Mecca, Mina, Arafat and different stages of the pilgrimage before the construction of the Hijaz Railway. The photographs, taken by the Meccan physician ʿAbd al-Ghaffar and later published by Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje, preserve a visual record of the journey and its rituals before modern rail transport transformed access to the Holy Cities. The attempted removal of ʿAbd al-Ghaffar’s signature also raises important questions about authorship and the European mediation of early photographic representations of the Hajj.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/a44.contextual_description: This painting demonstrates how Mecca’s urban and architectural structure was already the subject of careful documentation, planning and infrastructural concern well before the construction of the Hijaz Railway. It shows that the modernization of pilgrimage did not begin with the railway, but rather emerged from a longer process of rehabilitating, organizing and administrating the Holy Cities under Ottoman rule. By visually mapping the Masjid al-Haram within its urban context, the painting anticipates the later logic of connectivity and accessibility that the Hijaz Railway would institutionalize on a much larger scale.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/ecc.contextual_description: This illustrated architectural album records early European representations of Mecca and Medina, presenting the Holy Cities as subjects of architectural study long before the Hijaz Railway. Although partly inaccurate and shaped by second-hand sources, the views show how their urban and sacred architecture was already being documented, interpreted and circulated internationally.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/7bc.contextual_description: This plate from George Sale’s 1825 edition combines a plan and view of the Haram, identifying its principal sacred spaces. It shows Mecca as a city already being mapped and visually organised, while also reflecting a period before modern transport transformed access to the Holy City.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/7fb.contextual_description: This elevated view of the Masjid al-Haram and the Kaʿbah offers another perspective on Mecca’s sacred urban core. It documents the spatial relationship between the sanctuary and the surrounding city, helping to show how Mecca’s architecture and urban form were visually recorded before the transformations brought by modern transport.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/2f9.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme "Desert infrastructure and fortified railway architecture", shows how the Hijaz Railway adapted to remote and vulnerable desert environments. Qatranah serves as the main example, alongside stations such as Dhat Hajj and Antara and the earlier Qatrana fortress. Their architecture responds to the practical needs of protection, water supply, accommodation, storage and railway operations. Rather than monumental buildings, these stations functioned as self-sufficient infrastructural and defensive nodes that allowed the railway to operate across isolated territory.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/d5b.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme "Desert infrastructure and fortified railway architecture",  shows how the Hijaz Railway adapted to remote and vulnerable desert environments. Qatranah serves as the main example, alongside stations such as Dhat Hajj and Antara and the earlier Qatrana fortress. Their architecture responds to the practical needs of protection, water supply, accommodation, storage and railway operations. Rather than monumental buildings, these stations functioned as self-sufficient infrastructural and defensive nodes that allowed the railway to operate across isolated territory.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/68f.contextual_description: Dhat Hajj was already an important stop for caravans and pilgrims, valued for rest and water supplies, before the arrival of the Hijaz Railway. The railway increased its strategic importance, turning the site into a more permanent transport node adapted to the demands of travel across a remote desert landscape.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/2b0.contextual_description: The Antara locality provides another example of the remote landscape through which the Hijaz Railway operated. Seen alongside Qatranah and Dhat Hajj, it helps illustrate how railway infrastructure had to respond to isolated desert environments and create functional stopping points along the route.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/0d2.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme "Stations as urban and regional catalysts", shows how the Hijaz Railway reshaped existing settlements. Amman, Maʿan and Tabuk demonstrate how stations became centres of administration, trade, maintenance, accommodation and movement, generating new activity around them. Amman is particularly significant, as the arrival of the railway helped transform a relatively small settlement into an increasingly important regional centre.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/15a.contextual_description: Maʿan Station was one of the Hijaz Railway’s most important regional centres, combining passenger facilities, workshops, water infrastructure and staff accommodation. Like Amman, it shows how a railway station could generate a new concentration of movement, services, technical activity and administration around an existing settlement.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/bca.contextual_description: Maʿan Station was one of the Hijaz Railway’s most important regional centres, combining passenger facilities, workshops, water infrastructure and staff accommodation. Like Amman, it shows how a railway station could generate a new concentration of movement, services, technical activity and administration around an existing settlement.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/95e.contextual_description: Tabuk Station, set within an open desert landscape, shows how the Hijaz Railway created new centres of movement and service far from major cities. Its station building, curved track and nearby defensive blockhouse reflect the combination of transport, protection and regional connectivity that shaped railway growth along the route.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/270.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme "Oasis stations and archaeological landscapes", shows how the Hijaz Railway entered places already shaped by oases, historic settlements, pilgrimage routes and archaeological remains. Al-ʿUla and Mada’in Salih illustrate how modern railway infrastructure was inserted into long-established cultural landscapes, creating a new architectural layer within environments defined by much older patterns of settlement and movement.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/659.contextual_description: Mada’in Salih Station was one of the Hijaz Railway’s major stops, inserted into a landscape already shaped by ancient settlement, Nabataean monuments, pilgrimage routes, and water infrastructure. Its railway buildings added a new modern layer to a site with a much longer architectural and cultural history.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/f7a.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme “The monumental gateways”, brings together the Hijaz Railway’s most architecturally and symbolically important points of arrival and departure. Damascus is the principal example, while Medina and Bab ʿAnbari extend the idea toward the sacred destination of the line. Unlike smaller stations, these buildings functioned as urban gateways, announcing the railway within the city and expressing modernisation, imperial presence and new forms of mobility. Damascus, in particular, introduced a distinctive station typology that combined European railway planning with references to local Syrian architectural traditions.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/471.contextual_description: This group of images, presented under the theme “The monumental gateways”, brings together the Hijaz Railway’s most architecturally and symbolically important points of arrival and departure. 744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/8f9.contextual_description: Al-Madina al-Munawwara Station formed the southern terminus of the Hijaz Railway and one of its most important monumental gateways. Opened in 1908 near the Prophet’s Mosque, its extensive walled complex of eleven buildings announced the railway’s arrival in the Holy City and gave modern transport a strong architectural presence within Medina.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/9f8.contextual_description: Aleppo's Baghdad Railway Station was not part of the Hijaz Railway, but it offers a useful comparison within the wider Ottoman railway network. Completed in 1912, it functioned as a major urban gateway linking Aleppo with Anatolia and Mesopotamia, while helping generate a new modern district organised around transport and commerce.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/9cd.contextual_description: Aleppo's Baghdad Railway Station was not part of the Hijaz Railway, but it offers a useful comparison within the wider Ottoman railway network. 744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/54a.contextual_description: Haidar Pasha Station was not part of the Hijaz Railway, but it provides an important comparison within the wider Ottoman railway system. Rebuilt from 1906 as a monumental intermodal terminal linking rail, ferry and port traffic, it shows how stations became powerful architectural symbols of connectivity, modernisation and imperial ambition.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/366.contextual_description: Jerusalem, Jaffa and Ramleh stations were not part of the Hijaz Railway, but they provide an important parallel for understanding the wider impact of railway infrastructure on Ottoman cities. As the terminus of the Jaffa–Jerusalem line, the station introduced a new point of arrival into the urban fabric, linking the sacred city more directly to the coast and reshaping patterns of movement, trade and access. Seen alongside the Hijaz Railway, it illustrates how railway architecture became an instrument of urban transformation across the region.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/e3d.contextual_description: This painting of Haifa’s port illustrates how the Hijaz Railway transformed the city’s urban and economic importance. The branch linking Haifa to Darʿa connected the Mediterranean directly to the inland railway network, allowing pilgrims, travellers, and goods arriving by sea to continue toward Damascus and the Hijaz. The railway strengthened Haifa’s role as a regional transport hub, stimulated commercial and service activities, and contributed to the reorganisation and expansion of the urban fabric around the port and railway facilities.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/0e1.contextual_description: This photograph shows how closely Haifa's port and railway operated together. Passengers could arrive by sea and continue directly by train through Darʿa toward Damascus and the Hijaz, while the concentration of travellers also supported local trade, services, and tourism, strengthening Haifa’s role as a regional transport hub.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/a5d.contextual_description: This photograph shows how closely Haifa's port and railway operated together. Passengers could arrive by sea and continue directly by train through Darʿa toward Damascus and the Hijaz, while the concentration of travellers also supported local trade, services, and tourism, strengthening Haifa’s role as a regional transport hub.

Passengers could arrive by sea and continue directly by train through Darʿa toward Damascus and the Hijaz, while the concentration of travellers also supported local trade, services, and tourism, strengthening Haifa’s role as a regional transport hub.

744650c8-71c9-5cc3-9dec-e2fece5ed1e5/b67.contextual_description: El-Nassr Boulevard illustrates how the Hijaz Railway became a catalyst for urban transformation in Damascus. Widened and monumentalised during the First World War, the street connected the historic commercial centre near Suq al-Hamidiyya with the Hijaz Railway Station, creating a new urban axis through the city. Its scale and use for public celebrations contrasted with the narrow streets of the old city, showing how railway infrastructure encouraged new forms of planning, circulation, and public space in modern Damascus.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/1be.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway Photograph Album documents the railway crossing deserts, mountains and other harsh landscapes, where tracks, bridges and engineering works introduced a new technological presence into difficult terrain. The images present the railway as a striking symbol of Ottoman modernity, showing how steel, machinery and infrastructure were imposed upon and adapted to an environment long shaped by distance, isolation and natural obstacles

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/d4b.contextual_description: This 1906 image documents the ballasting of the Hijaz Railway track bed during construction. It reveals the practical labour behind the line, showing how the desert landscape had to be physically prepared and stabilised before the rails could operate, turning difficult terrain into modern railway infrastructure.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/8ba.contextual_description: This 1906 image documents the ballasting of the Hijaz Railway track bed during construction. It reveals the practical labour behind the line, showing how the desert landscape had to be physically prepared and stabilised before the rails could operate, turning difficult terrain into modern railway infrastructure.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/a2c.contextual_description: Tadarees Bridge illustrates how the Hijaz Railway adapted modern engineering to the harsh terrain of north-western Arabia. Built to carry the line across a wadi between Tabuk and al-ʿUla, the stone bridge transformed a natural obstacle into part of the railway network. It reflects the technical ambition of the project and the effort required to extend modern infrastructure through remote and challenging landscapes.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/535.contextual_description: This bridge at kilometre 378 from Damascus illustrates the engineering solutions required to carry the Hijaz Railway across difficult terrain. Like Tadarees Bridge, it shows how bridges became essential elements in adapting the railway to the varied landscapes encountered along the route.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/e95.contextual_description: This filled embankment shows how the railway landscape itself had to be reshaped to create a stable route for the tracks. Such earthworks were essential in negotiating uneven ground and demonstrate the large-scale engineering required to extend the Hijaz Railway across difficult terrain.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/6d0.contextual_description: This six-span bridge at kilometre 403 from Damascus demonstrates the range of engineering structures required along the Hijaz Railway. Its repeated spans allowed the track to cross uneven terrain while maintaining a stable route, reflecting the technical planning behind the railway’s construction.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/d28.contextual_description: This iron bridge near Haifa illustrates the use of modern construction technology on the Darʿa–Haifa branch of the Hijaz Railway. Together with other bridges, tunnels, and stations documented in the album, it shows the engineering effort required to connect the Mediterranean coast with the inland railway network.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/35f.contextual_description: This postcard shows a major viaduct on the Haifa–Darʿa section of the Hijaz Railway, presenting substantial railway engineering within the Palestinian landscape. Its circulation as a postcard also transformed technical infrastructure into a visible symbol of modernity, connectivity, and construction achievement.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/81d.contextual_description: This photograph records the construction of a bridge near Haifa, revealing the labour and engineering processes behind the finished railway infrastructure. Rather than showing only the completed structure, it highlights the practical work required to overcome difficult terrain and extend the Hijaz Railway network.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/c8d.contextual_description: This image shows a train decorated with Ottoman flags during the ceremonial opening of a railway bridge, with passengers and dignitaries gathered on the structure. Beyond its technical function, the bridge became a public symbol of engineering progress, connectivity, and Ottoman modernity.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/27d.contextual_description: This view of the Hijazi landscape evokes the remote and harsh environment through which the railway was constructed. Mountains, desert and long distances formed natural obstacles that modern engineering had to overcome. Seen alongside images of tracks, bridges and trains, the landscape highlights the dramatic arrival of modern technology in the Hijaz and the transformation of previously difficult terrain into a connected railway corridor.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/8e4.contextual_description: This map presents the Hijaz Railway as a modern infrastructure imposed across a vast and varied landscape of deserts, mountains, towns and ports. By tracing the line from Damascus toward Medina and recording each station through measured distances, it transforms geography into an organised and connected network. The bilingual Ottoman Turkish and Arabic labels further reflect the administrative and technological modernity through which the empire sought to understand, measure and connect its territories.

47c76d39-06fe-58c3-b694-73c081518a4d/35a.contextual_description: This view of Darʿa captures the encounter between older forms of movement and the new railway age. A camel caravan crosses the landscape near one of the most important junctions of the Hijaz Railway, where routes toward Palestine and the Hijaz intersected. The image contrasts traditional desert transport with the expanding railway network, symbolising the arrival of modern infrastructure within a landscape still shaped by long-established patterns of travel and exchange.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/76d.contextual_description: These bridal cushions from Ma'an, Jordan, reflect how the city's importance as a stop on pilgrimage and trade routes, before and after construction of the Hijaz Railway, resulted in the dispersion of crafts from the wider Levant, the Caucasus, and Central Asia. Influences from these regions helped to make Ma'ani traditional crafts vibrant and distinct throughout Jordan.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/f30.contextual_description: An example of architectural styles brought together by exchanges among people from different religions, cultures, and ethnicities under the Ottoman Empire. Dar Al-Baladiya, which served as a municipal building, was built in Damascus in a European-inspired Ottoman style. Incorporating Syria's own stone-cutting crafts, it presented a mix of local and global traditions as the city's town hall.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/a8a.contextual_description: Completed in 1884, Suq al-Hamidyya is the largest souq in Syria and still operates today. At 600 metres long, its entrance lies approximately 1km away from the Hijaz Train Station. Travellers from modern-day Jordan and the Hijaz region would have had easy access to the unique works sold at the souk, including traditional textiles.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/ecb.contextual_description: People walking near Jaffa Gate, Jerusalem, circa 1917. While most are local city-dwellers, one European man can be noted on the far left. People in the city were mainly craftsmen or merchants.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/0ec.contextual_description: An insight into the towns, villages, and cities built under the Ottoman Empire in the Levant and the regions surrounding the Hijaz Railway. Landscapes began to be urbanised in the 19th century in the Ottoman Levant, but agriculture and rural life remained economically and culturally important.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/42d.contextual_description: A photograph of the pilgrims beginning their journey from Istanbul, where they would embark on the train to Damascus, then switch to the Hijaz Railway. Damascus had connections to Lebanon and parts of northern Palestine, making it easy for passengers to continue their journeys.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/a9d.contextual_description: The enamelled clock face of this pocket watch has an image of a Hijaz Railway engine and the Ottoman coat of arms. This was likely made for an Ottoman official involved in the building of the railway.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/c87.contextual_description: This ihram belt would have been worn by a male pilgrim and used to hold valuables while he performed the Hajj rites. The ihram garment for men consists of two pieces of unstitched white cloth. It would be considered an essential garment to bring on a journey to Mecca.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/6b9.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway, which crossed borders and regions, provided passengers with exposure to clothing of various villages and groups. This was particularly true in the Levant, known for its people from diverse religious, ethnic, and linguistic backgrounds. This dagger is an example of a traditional accessory of Jordanian Bedouins and villagers, and might have been worn by a train passenger.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/15b.contextual_description: A simple leather item used by people across the territories of the Hijaz Railway. Many stations would have wells or water sources for passengers. This was particularly important as they entered the increasingly arid landscapes of the south.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/5b3.contextual_description: This water bottle would have been an important part of every pilgrim’s luggage. Collecting water, sharing it with loved ones, and gifting it is an old tradition that resulted in the widespread transportation of Zamzam water: blessed water from Mecca.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/8ce.contextual_description: A small and simple bag made of materials common to the Levant and wider territories – particularly the silver coins, which were more commonly sewn into headdresses and clothing to demonstrate wealth, or as a portable dowry. Though small, the bag could have been used by travellers to carry cosmetic products.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/24d.contextual_description: Small bags like this one were carried by travellers to keep valuables close at hand. Designed to hold jewellery, money, cosmetics or perfume, it provided security and convenience on a journey.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/89d.contextual_description: Horse jewellery was common across Bedouin and village communities in the region. This amulet was used to ward off misfortune. Made of silver and boar tusk and featuring a one-quarter Majidi Ottoman gold coin, it represents the life of the region and the value placed on horses.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/0fd.contextual_description: Ottoman coins circulated widely across the Arab provinces, facilitating trade, taxation, travel and everyday exchanges. Along the Hijaz Railway, fares, salaries and administrative accounts were calculated in Ottoman currency, and travellers used coins for transport, food, accommodations and goods.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/00f.contextual_description: Tell el-Hesi was the first major archaeological excavation site in Palestine, conducted by the Palestine Exploration Fund. The diggers in the photograph are native men, women, and children. Until 1938, all worked together. Note the clothing worn by the working families. An amulet or necklace can be seen on the second person from the left.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/918.contextual_description: The incorporation of various groups’ fashions into traditional clothing in Jordan is evidence of how the new railway shaped people’s interactions with other groups and influenced styles in the last century.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/59f.contextual_description: The incorporation of various groups' fashions into traditional clothing in Jordan is evidence of how the railway shaped people's interactions in new ways outside their own groups. This dress is made of silk produced in Syria and traded in Palestine and Jordan.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/683.contextual_description: The use of Ottoman and Russian coins in this headdress reflects the changing demographics and movement of people in Jordan in the early 20th century. The Hijaz Railway enabled travel from distant countries into Jordan, as people from all over made their way to Damascus, and from there by rail to Medina.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/e17.contextual_description: This ornamental accessory reflects the diverse nature of trade, travel, beliefs and traditions across the Levantine region at this time. The historical coins are evidence of the wide-ranging movement of people and goods into the region. The blue pieces function as amulets to protect a bride from the evil eye, blue being a colour typically associated with protection across the Mediterranean region.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/002.contextual_description: This attire is representative of the working-class population in Lebanon in the 19th century, though similar garments and styles would have been seen across the region at this time.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/124.contextual_description: An illustration of a man named Muhammad Ali, a calligrapher in 19th-century Palestine. He is possibly linked to, or the son of, Baha'ullah, founder of the Baha'i faith. His calligraphic style emulates the bold style developed by the Baha'i faith's primary calligrapher, Mirza Husain Isfahani Mishkin Qalam. This sketch illustrates the appearance of someone who may have used the items seen in this section of the exhibition.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/6d3.contextual_description: This asbe, a traditional Jordanian headpiece, is evidence of the deep ties Levantine countries share, and of movement and trade among them. A key Jordanian tradition, the asbe was crafted from Syrian fabric and reminds us that craftsmanship moved across borders in response to demand and developing practices.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/35a.contextual_description: In Islamic popular belief blue eyes are thought to be envious. This ‘eye of envy’ is worn to repel negative power by reflecting the perpetrator’s own envy, protecting the wearer from the effects of jealousy, thought to cause illness or disaster. With its spiritual powers this talisman might have been carried on journeys for good luck.

70a44ddf-91b4-5789-9087-b25d0f0d84c8/944.contextual_description: Embellishing accessories and clothing with coins was a common practice across the Levant, using coins from a wide variety of places and periods. This is evidence of diverse trade and movement across the region during this Ottoman period.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/2e9.contextual_description: A postcard of Straight Street, Damascus' *decumanus maximus*, and one of the oldest inhabited streets in the world. On the western side is the Midhat Pasha Souq, which included a silk bazaar that sold imported clothing from Lebanon, along with keffiyehs and general food items.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/9fb.contextual_description: Money has always been essential on any journey. Necessary for food, shelter, and souvenirs, travellers must carry it on their persons. Ottoman currency was used across the empire – not just for trade, but also incorporated into wearable dowries and accessories.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/ec7.contextual_description: Though these tiles were made long before the construction of the Hijaz Railway, they reflect the long-standing Damascene tradition of craftsmanship. These goods would circulate in the Islamic and Ottoman worlds, connecting to Damascus and emphasising its importance as a crossroads of artisanal trade.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/c50.contextual_description: These carpets, made in Syria during the 16th and 17th centuries, reflect Damascus’ longstanding tradition and expertise in craftsmanship. The geometric designs are imitations of more complex chessboard carpets made for courts in previous centuries. They were woven to meet the huge appetite for this type of carpet in Western Europe, and are a reminder of Damascus’ importance as a crossroads of cultural exchange between Ottoman and European regions.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/db8.contextual_description: Belonging to Bedouin communities of the Naqab Desert, this is an example of the coin-adorned accessories common in Palestine and the wider Levant region, rooted in a history of displaying wealth and being a part of a visual dowry. The coins would have been sourced from different time periods and places, reflecting the diversity of communities and movement of people and goods.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/666.contextual_description: Coins did not circulate only as money. As they moved between regions and communities they could acquire new functions and meanings. Incorporated into dress and personal adornment, coins became portable forms of wealth as well as visible markers of identity. The presence of coins from different places can also reflect the wider networks of trade and mobility that connected communities across the region.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/1ba.contextual_description: The Syrian silk used to make this flag reflects the movement of materials across the region and the wider networks of trade and exchange that connected communities along the railway.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/830.contextual_description: The sarma is an Ottoman metallic-thread embroidery technique employed in urban communities for elite and festive dress. Travelling from the Ottoman centre to Levantine urban hubs such as Jerusalem, Jaffa, and Damascus, it is evidence of the movement and adoption of various cultural crafts into urban centres due to the ease of transportation.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/207.contextual_description: Ma'an has some of the most vibrantly coloured costumes in modern-day Jordan due to its importance as a stop along the Hijaz Railway. Earlier it had been a stop on pilgrimage and caravan routes to Mecca. One of the final stations before the Hijaz region, Ma'an was where many tradesmen, especially Syrians, sold goods to finance the rest of their journey. Syrian textiles typically featured more colourful and patterned designs than those found in the rest of Jordan.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/bf1.contextual_description: These bridal cushions are examples of Ma'an's importance as a stop along pilgrimage and trade routes. The embroidered designs and use of ikat textiles represent the blend of cultural crafts found in Ma'an, which adopted textile traditions from Central Asia, Türkiye, and Syria.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/9a8.contextual_description: These bridal cushions represent the importance of Ma'an as a trading stop on the traditional pilgrimage route during the operation of the Hijaz Railway and earlier. The embroidery patterns featured have links to the Caucasus region and show how vibrant cultural features were absorbed into local artistic practices.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/955.contextual_description: This cap is remarkable for the way it represents the frequency of trade and transport in its time as a result of the Hijaz and other railways. It was made in Azerbaijan but found in Palestine, an indication of the vast area of Ottoman influence and exchange.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/d02.contextual_description: Haifa railway station was built in 1905. It was the terminus of the Haifa branch of the Hijaz Railway, connecting the Mediterranean port with the main railway line at Daraa. This commemorative postcard frames the station with colourful Ottoman postage stamps, flags and imperial emblems. The image celebrates the railway as an achievement of Ottoman modernisation, communication and connectivity across the empire.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/87b.contextual_description: These postcards show how the Hijaz Railway linked people, money and goods across borders. The French and Turkish postcards, made in Germany and sold at post offices, were themselves objects of exchange: they raised funds, spread images of the railway across the empire and beyond, and circulated through the postal network, showing how technology, commerce and faith moved together.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/11a.contextual_description: The monument near the Damascus Railway station that commemorates the installation of the Hijaz-Damascus telegraph connection. It opened shortly before the inauguration of the railway to strengthen communication through and alongside it. It is also a physical representation of communications facilitated by the railway.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/317.contextual_description: This postcard documents some of the sites passengers could see on arriving in Medina. Many of these landmarks were destroyed in 1926. Produced for travellers as a keepsake of their journey, the postcard serves as a valuable visual record of the city’s historic landscape, preserving a view of Medina as it appeared to those who passed through it.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/4cb.contextual_description: This postcard reflects the significance of the Hijaz Railway station in the modernising urban landscape of Damascus. Its production is an example of how images of railway architecture were collected and circulated, extending the influence of the railway beyond the journey itself.

0593ab8d-bef3-5793-857c-0dc9a8f95ab4/32b.contextual_description: For centuries, pilgrims travelled to the Hijaz in organised caravans, including on major routes from Cairo and Damascus. This late 19th- or early 20th-century painting by British artist Robert Murdoch Wright depicts the Egyptian Hajj caravan leaving Bab al-Nasr. Such works reflect Western artists’ growing interest in the region, transforming travel scenes into lasting visual records.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/fc0.contextual_description: The palace became an important administrative centre under Sultan Abdülhamid II, during whose reign the Hijaz Railway was conceived and constructed. Under his reign the railway was connected to Istanbul, the Ottoman imperial capital where the project was promoted and administered.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/cc6.contextual_description: Built between 1903 and 1909, during the same period as the Hijaz Railway, the Istanbul Main Post Office is an example of modern communication infrastructure in the late Ottoman Empire. Postal and railway networks enhanced connectivity across Ottoman territories, facilitating the movement of people, information and correspondence.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/c08.contextual_description: A major centre of commerce in the Ottoman capital, the Grand Bazaar brought together merchants, craftspeople, travellers and goods from different regions. Its long-established networks of trade and exchange continued alongside the expanding railway and communication networks of the late Ottoman period.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/e6a.contextual_description: Bab al-Jabiya connected Damascus’s urban and commercial life with older routes of pilgrimage and travel. The market that extended from the gate served pilgrims and travelling merchants heading south towards Mecca, movement that long predated the Hijaz Railway.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/603.contextual_description: Khan al-Harir reveals the commercial world that travellers encountered in Damascus. Combining accommodation, workshops and wholesale trade, the 16th-century silk caravanserai brought merchants, craftspeople and goods together in the city, encounters that long predated the railway.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/c8b.contextual_description: Hammams were an important part of urban life, offering residents and travellers places to wash, rest and refresh themselves. For those arriving after long journeys, they formed part of the network of services and social spaces in the city.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/c18.contextual_description: A major Ottoman complex on the historic Hajj route, Takiyya al-Sulaymaniyya provided accommodations, food and support to pilgrims and travellers. It reflects Damascus’s long-standing role as a major gathering and departure point, where travellers prepared for journeys towards the Hijaz and the Holy Cities.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/4c3.contextual_description: A major religious and architectural landmark of Damascus, the Umayyad Mosque reflects the city’s deep historical layers. For pilgrims preparing to travel on the Hijaz Railway, Damascus was the starting point of the journey, and visits to sites such as the mosque were part of the pilgrim’s preparation for the long trip south towards the Holy Cities.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/474.contextual_description: Originally built as the residence of Yusuf Anbar, a wealthy Damascene Jewish merchant, Maktab Anbar was later acquired by the Ottoman authorities and converted into a modern state school. Its transformation reflects both Damascus’s diverse communities and the wider educational and institutional modernisation taking place alongside new transport and communication networks.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/1e1.contextual_description: Built in 1900 under Ottoman patronage, Hamadi Hospital reflects the changing urban landscape of Damascus as the Hijaz Railway was being developed. The hospital represents the expansion of modern civic and healthcare institutions alongside new transport and communication infrastructure, evidence of a city undergoing significant transformation.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/f19.contextual_description: Dating to the 18th century, Beit Nizam takes its name from the Nizam family, its occupants in the early 20th century. Its richly decorated courtyards and reception rooms display craftsmanship, domestic life and social history in Damascus, revealing another layer of the rich heritage of city dwellers.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/e3c.contextual_description: Founded in the 12th century by Nur al-Din, the Bimaristan reflects Damascus’s long tradition of medicine, learning and public welfare. Its survival into the age of the Hijaz Railway reveals the historical layers of the city, where centuries-old institutions and architecture coexisted with new forms of transport, communication and civic institutions.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/0ed.contextual_description: The Mausoleum of Salah al-Din reveals the layered heritage of Damascus. It is an Ayyubid monument enriched by later Ottoman interventions and a marble cenotaph associated with Emperor Wilhelm II’s 1898 visit. Centuries of international encounters shaped Damascus long before the construction of the Hijaz Railway.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/c37.contextual_description: Located on long-established caravan and pilgrimage routes to Mecca, Bosra was an important stopping point for travellers journeying south. Its citadel, churches, mosques and ancient remains are evidence of the city’s historical and cultural heritage.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/c29.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway was part of a wider network of railways transforming the region. Opened in 1895, the connection from the Mediterranean port of Beirut to Damascus facilitated movement between the coast and the interior. The line reinforced Beirut’s role as a major commercial gateway, and reflected European competition over transport routes and regional trade.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/901.contextual_description: Though the port of Beirut is over 3,500 years old, its modern commercial history begins in 1887, when the Ottomans granted it to a French company and gave it increasing autonomy. The port was extremely important, bringing travellers and goods into the Levant and the wider region.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/991.contextual_description: The headquarters of the railway company that operated the Beirut–Damascus line was part of the infrastructure behind the growing regional railway network. The line connected Beirut with Damascus and onward to the Hijaz, and reinforced Beirut’s economic importance as a major Mediterranean port.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/e35.contextual_description: The Grand Serail has a rich history as one of the important Ottoman monuments on Serail Hill. Originally established as a military barracks, it later housed civilian departments and Ottoman governors, evidence of Beirut’s growing administrative importance. Adapted and expanded over time, its prominent location made it a defining feature of the late Ottoman city.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/567.contextual_description: Saint George Maronite Cathedral reflects Beirut’s religious diversity and the important presence of its Maronite community. Its Neoclassical architecture, inspired by European models, reveals wider cultural and architectural connections between Beirut and the Mediterranean world.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/d70.contextual_description: The National Evangelical Church reflects the religious diversity of Ottoman Beirut, where various faiths and Christian denominations formed distinct communities and places of worship. Such religious institutions were part of the diverse social and urban landscape encountered by those living in and travelling through the city.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/02c.contextual_description: Beaufort Castle (Qalʿat al-Shaqif) reflects the history of a region shaped by centuries of movement, conflict and change. Successively occupied and transformed under different powers, it reveals the layered political and cultural history of territories through which modern transport networks would later develop. Unfortunately, this important historical monument was damaged during the recent Israeli war on Lebanon.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/b25.contextual_description: The Jaffa–Jerusalem railway, opened in 1892, connected the important Mediterranean port of Jaffa with Jerusalem. *Palestine Past and Present*, a book by Laura Jewry Valentine, follows this railway journey, describing places and landscapes along this route, part of the expanding transport networks of late Ottoman Palestine.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/526.contextual_description: Bab al-Khalil is a principal gateway to Jerusalem through which pilgrims, merchants and other travellers connected the historic city with wider transportation routes across Palestine.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/582.contextual_description: The Citadel of Jerusalem is a major landmark reflecting the city’s layered history and its rich architectural heritage. Its towers and walls rose above the Old City beside the Jaffa Gate, one of the first sights for travellers arriving from the coast.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/065.contextual_description: Jerusalem was part of the wider sacred geography of Muslim pilgrimage. Pilgrims travelling to or returning from the Hajj could visit the holy sites of Jerusalem, adding the city to the broader pilgrimage network served by the Hijaz Railway.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/cca.contextual_description: This mosque is one of Islam’s holiest sites and a major destination for pilgrimage and religious travel, evidence of Jerusalem’s significance in the sacred and cultural landscape of Palestine and the wider Abrahamic world. Travellers from across the Hijaz took advantage of the railway to visit the mosque and other historical and religious monuments.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/930.contextual_description: An example of the rich architectural and educational heritage of Jerusalem’s Old City, the madrasa reflects the city’s long history as a centre of religious learning, pilgrimage and cultural encounter. Existing in different forms since 901/1496, this madrasa was a foundational part of life in Jerusalem.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/a04.contextual_description: Before 1967, a narrow prayer space beside the al-Buraq Wall bordered the historic Maghribi Quarter, a waqf associated with North African Muslims and pilgrims. The wall was also a place of prayer for Jerusalem’s Jewish community. In June 1967, the Maghribi Quarter was demolished to create the present Western Wall Plaza.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/e6e.contextual_description: This site is associated with Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions, reflecting Jerusalem’s layered sacred landscape, its importance to pilgrims and visitors of different faiths, and the vibrant diversity in beliefs and customs across the city and beyond.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/952.contextual_description: A major destination of Christian pilgrimage for centuries, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre reflects Jerusalem’s place within long-established networks of religious travel and encounter. In the early 20th century, new railways and steamship routes brought growing numbers of visitors to the city, continuing the movement of generations of pilgrims.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/1d2.contextual_description: The Church of the Tomb of Mary is a historic Christian pilgrimage site, reflecting the sacred landscape and long traditions of religious travel that connected Jerusalem with pilgrims from across the region and beyond. Located at the foot of the Mount of Olives, it was among the sites visited by travellers in the Holy Land.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/528.contextual_description: Suq al-Qattanin, the Cotton Merchants’ Market, was a major commercial street in the Old City, directly connected to Al-Haram al-Sharif. It developed from the close relationships among trade, urban life and sacred spaces in Jerusalem. Travellers and pilgrims would have encountered its covered lanes and busy shops on the way to the sanctuary, an aspect of everyday life around holy places.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/5f9.contextual_description: The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem is a major destination of Christian pilgrimage, reflecting the diverse sacred geography and centuries-old traditions of travel that shaped Palestine long before the railway age. Built over the traditional birthplace of Jesus, it continued to draw visitors as new means of transportation facilitated journeys to the Holy Land.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/eaf.contextual_description: A major pilgrimage site associated with Abrahamic traditions, it reflects the layered sacred landscape and long-established networks of religious travel in Palestine, made significantly more accessible via new methods of transportation.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/5ea.contextual_description: A historic commercial market reflecting the importance of trade and mercantile life in the city. With a name literally related to tradesmen, this suq was the most widely used and economically active in Nablus, an important stop on historical trade routes in Palestine. Merchants commonly travelled there on Ottoman railways.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/3a1.contextual_description: The Tomb of Joseph in Nablus is a sacred site associated with the biblical figure Joseph and is revered by different religious traditions. It reflects the layered religious heritage of Nablus and the wider sacred geography of Palestine, where pilgrimage and local traditions connected communities and places across the region.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/a5f.contextual_description: The Great ‘Umari Mosque was a major landmark of Gaza, a city long situated on routes connecting Egypt, Palestine and Syria. Gaza’s position attracted merchants, travellers and pilgrims, making it an important place of trade, movement and encounter. The historic mosque was severely damaged by Israeli bombardment during the recent war in Gaza, marking a profound loss to the city’s architectural and cultural heritage.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/e40.contextual_description: Dating to the Mamluk period, Hammam al-Samara served Gaza’s inhabitants and visitors. As a place for bathing, rest and social interaction, it reflects urban life and the services available in a city frequented by merchants, travellers and pilgrims moving along regional routes.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/828.contextual_description: Claude R. Conder, a British Royal Engineers officer, travelled through Palestine while working on the Palestine Exploration Fund’s *Survey of Western Palestine* in the 1870s. His watercolours documented local landscapes, settlements and people. Painted in 1872, this view records a landscape that predates the railway age, offering a glimpse of the territories through which new transport networks would develop.

9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/347.contextual_description: Rising above Amman, the Citadel reflects the city’s long and layered history, with remains from successive periods and cultures. As Amman developed into an important station on the Hijaz Railway, this ancient landmark stood alongside a changing urban landscape, connecting the city’s deep past with new networks of movement and exchange.
