9922819a-39a2-564b-9bb6-55ddbad28666/d5b.contextual_description: Built in 1531 under Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent, Qatrana Fortress and its reservoir provided water, protection and supplies along the pilgrimage route to Mecca and Medina. It is part of the infrastructure that sustained long-distance pilgrimage through Jordan centuries before the Hijaz Railway transformed travel along this historic corridor.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/a13.contextual_description: This blueprint of the Hijaz Railway reflects many important points of history in the design of the Hijaz Railway project. Signed by the German Heinrich August Meissner, it shows the influence and involvement of European powers in the Ottoman world before and after the design and construction of the railway, and also after the Arab Revolt, when sections of it were bombed and trains fell into disuse.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/0f6.contextual_description: This train station linked the port of Beirut to its main station, allowing rapid movement between maritime and land routes for goods and passengers continuing to Damascus. It contributed to Beirut’s status as the primary port of the region.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/8cf.contextual_description: Built by a French civil engineering company under Ottoman rule, this train station had two lines: one to Damascus and one across the coast to Palestine. It combines French architectural styles with Levantine industrial requirements and materials. It made train travel from Istanbul to the Palestinian coastal cities possible through the wider Ottoman rail network.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/fcf.contextual_description: The iconic Damascus station, commonly known as al-Hamidiyah (Hamidiye) Station, where many travellers began the journey to Medina via the Hejaz Railway. Damascus had railway connections to Istanbul, Beirut, Haifa, and other cities. The Damascus station is a grand building with an iconic facade that incorporates early 20th-century European architecture into traditional Ottoman style. It was designed by Spanish architect Fernando de Aranda. The building is a testament to the European-Ottoman collaboration that made the Hijaz Railway possible.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/43d.contextual_description: Travel on the Hijaz Railway varied according to class, with tickets issued for first- and third-class travel. During the busy pilgrimage season, carriages could become extremely crowded. A. J. B. Wavell, who travelled from Damascus to Medina in 1908, described crowded wagons carrying pilgrims of different backgrounds and languages alongside Ottoman soldiers. His account captures the diversity of passengers as well as the discomfort, uncertainty and emotional experience of travelling towards the Hijaz.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/0d2.contextual_description: The Amman station was an important stop on the Hijaz Railway, connecting the growing town with Damascus to the north and destinations south towards Medina. Opened in 1903, the station supported the movement of passengers, pilgrims, and goods.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/15a.contextual_description: Ma’an Station would have been a notable landmark for passengers traveling by train along the route, visually affirming the scale and modernity of the railway project and underscoring its role as a facilitator of progress and connectivity in the region.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/556.contextual_description: One of the last stops in Jordan before the route entered the Hijaz, Al-Mudawwara had served travellers along the Hajj route for centuries. The complex, associated with the pilgrimage route from at least the ninth century, and rebuilt during the Ottoman period, included a fortress, water reservoir and paved road. These structures provided water, shelter and greater security for travellers journeying through the desert. The Hijaz Railway followed and transformed an ancient pilgrimage corridor rather than creating a new route.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/aad.contextual_description: This photograph album commemorates the Hijaz Railway as one of the major projects of its time. Its images document the scale of its construction, the stations and engineering works built along the route, and the varied landscapes through which the railway passed. Together the images provide a visual journey along the line and a record of the people and expertise behind its construction.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/68f.contextual_description: Long established as a place of rest for travellers on the way to pilgrimage, with a water tank and nearby Islamic fort, the station was constructed on the railway due to its historical position as a caravan stop. The village it is in grew in importance with the arrival of the Hijaz Railway, as pilgrims and traders needing accommodations arrived from the north.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/a2c.contextual_description: Situated between the Tabuk and al-Ula stations, this stone bridge is an example of the materials, design and construction required to make the Hijaz Railway operational. Still standing today, it reflects the robustness of the original design.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/659.contextual_description: One of the main railway stations, Mada'in Salih contained five wells, perfect for passengers taking a break, debarking at the station, or preparing to go north. With an ancient Islamic castle on the property, it shows how stations were strategically placed near and along existing routes and in significant locations.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/270.contextual_description: Al Ula station was an important stop in the southern section of the Hijaz Railway, near the historical oasis of Al Ula. The station provided water and services essential to the steam locomotives and to travellers crossing the increasingly arid landscape towards Medina.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/8f9.contextual_description: Medina marked the southern terminus of the Hijaz Railway, completed in 1908. The final section, from al-ʿUla to the holy city, was constructed exclusively by Muslim engineers and workers. The large station complex, enclosed by a black basalt wall, comprised eleven buildings and provided the infrastructure needed for arriving trains and travellers. Although the railway was intended to continue to Mecca, the extension was never completed, and pilgrims made the final stage of their journey via established land routes.

a9b7a575-60fd-5fe3-b5be-a36edd80fdd4/8fb.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway reached Medina in 1908, but the planned extension to Mecca was never completed. For pilgrims travelling on to Mecca the railway journey ended at Medina and the pilgrimage continued via traditional land routes. This 19th-century view evokes the landscape and environment of the pilgrimage’s ultimate destination.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/f03.contextual_description: The San Remo Conference in April 1920 was a post-WWI meeting of the Allied powers that finalized the distribution of former Ottoman territories in the Middle East. It officially assigned the mandates for Palestine and Mesopotamia to Great Britain and for Syria and Lebanon to France. Rooted in the Sykes–Picot plan and the Balfour Declaration, these decisions also determined the future of Ottoman infrastructure such as the Hijaz Railway through border creation. The empty seats in this photograph highlight the absence of actors from the region to advocate their interests at this meeting.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/97c.contextual_description: The subtitle for this image from the San Remo conference in 1920 is “The Conference of the Four Nation.” Delegates from Britain, France, Italy, and Japan met to discuss the territorial dissolution of former Ottoman lands. Despite the name, the United States also sent delegates in an observer capacity to the meeting. Although the conference is most known for the creation of the Mandate system in the Middle East, Britain and France also agreed to the San Remo Oil Agreement at the same time, transferring shares from the Deutsche Bank in the Turkish Petroleum Company to Allied powers.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/35b.contextual_description: The San Remo Conference in April, 1920 was a post-WWI meeting of the Allied powers that finalized the distribution of former Ottoman territories in the Middle East. It officially assigned the mandates for Palestine and Mesopotamia to Great Britain and for Syria and Lebanon to France. Rooted in the Sykes–Picot plan and the Balfour Declaration, these decisions also determined the future of Ottoman infrastructure such as the Hijaz Railway. The empty seats in this photograph highlight the absence of actors from the region to advocate their interests at this meeting.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/ed6.contextual_description: This gold dinar was struck in Makkah during the reign of Sharif Hussein bin Ali, leader of the Arab Revolt and later King of the Hijaz (1916–1924). Its inscriptions proclaim Hussein’s authority and even his claim to the caliphate, reflecting his bid for both political and religious legitimacy after the fall of Ottoman rule.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/00a.contextual_description: This gold dinar, minted in Mecca in AH 1334 (1916), marked the proclamation of Hussein bin ‘Ali as “King” of the Arab countries during the Arab Revolt. While the coin’s inscription celebrated him as leader of an Arab resistance, Britain, France and Italy only recognized him as King of the Hijaz. More than currency, the dinar embodies the struggle over political legitimacy and the contested ambitions of Arab independence amid the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/766.contextual_description: This silver coin was issued under Abdulaziz Ibn Saud, who conquered the Hijaz in 1925 and unified much of the Arabian Peninsula. Unlike Hussein’s purely calligraphic design, it combines inscriptions with palm trees and crossed swords, symbols that later became national emblems of Saudi Arabia.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/11a.contextual_description: This postcard shows the Hijaz Railway Monument in Damascus, a tall commemorative column erected in 1908 in front of the Hijaz Railway Station to celebrate the completion of the line under Sultan Abdülhamid II. It offers a glimpse of a fragmented recent past for the railway, which was no longer in operation after the end of the First World War.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/e28.contextual_description: This postcard depicts Amman's Third Circle and the Shmeisani tunnel during an era of rapid urban modernization. Beyond serving as a traffic solution, the roundabout functioned as a space for constructing urban identity. At its center stands a monument bearing the inscription "Allah, Homeland, King," projecting state ideology into the public sphere. The square thus represents the convergence of modern urban planning and political messaging, capturing Amman's evolving character in both social and symbolic dimensions.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/89c.contextual_description: A postcard went from Robin to a Mr. Paul Ashbee in Norwich details the tourist path a British traveller to Syria followed. We see from the letter that Robin visited Aleppo and Damascus and will journey on from the ancient city of Palmyra to Homs, the castle of Krak des Chevaliers, the port city of Latakia, and the ancient site of Ugarit. The stamp in the upper right corner shows the postage from the Syrian Arab Republic.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/05d.contextual_description: This 1966 photograph depicts Mecca in the wake of the post-war urbanization boom that reshaped the city's built environment. By this period, most pilgrims arrived for Hajj via buses, airplanes, and ships, marking a shift away from rail travel and traditional camel caravans that had historically defined the pilgrimage journey. Despite this shift, Mecca continued its rapid expansion, accommodating both its growing permanent population and the influx of pilgrims arriving annually, underscoring the city's evolving role as a modern urban centre and enduring site of religious significance.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/5d2.contextual_description: This Iraqi half dinar banknote, issued in 1945 (AH 1364) by Bradbury Wilkinson & Co. in England, features ornate Arabic calligraphy at the centre and a portrait of the young King Faisal II on the right. Produced little more than a decade after Iraq’s independence in 1932, it symbolizes both the consolidation of the Hashemite monarchy in Iraq and the emergence of national identity through state currency.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/d6d.contextual_description: Issued following Jordan's independence in 1946, this banknote features the Treasury of Petra. By placing Petra at the heart of its national currency, the Hashemite Kingdom positioned archaeology as a symbol of modern identity and continuity of an esteemed past. As with banknotes elsewhere, heritage served as a visual language for nation-building and cultural pride.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/58c.contextual_description: This photo displays a pro-independence protest in Syria from 1920. Waves of protests and revolutions in the region spoke to the hope of a new region after the withdraw of Ottoman power. Protests like this issued in a wave of nationalism and anti-imperialism, fundamentally altering the geo-political borders of the Middle East.

e23386c4-18a5-5c2e-a397-0d21a1c3d559/a5f.contextual_description: This historic reservoir in the southern Syrian city of Bosra served as a reprovisioning spot for hajj caravans. The Ayyubid ruler, al-Mu’azzem ‘Isa constructed a reservoir in the area to assist pilgrims traveling to Hajj as far back as the 13th century. Ibn Battuta, the famous traveller, mentions the reservoir at Bosra as it attracted local Hourani merchants to peddle their goods to pilgrims, making the stop not only about water but a larger economic zone to bolster provisions.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/4f8.contextual_description: Horses, camels, and mules were the traditional means of travel for nomadic and seminomadic groups in the Hijaz and Levant for generations. While the Hijaz Railway meant to industrialize the pilgrim travel from Damascus to Medina, quadrupeds remained an essential part of the pilgrimage route as well as vital resources for the construction of the railroad itself. While the railway served as a mechanized replacement for their labour, horses and camels remained vital to the path of the railway before, during, and after its construction.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/967.contextual_description: A zoomorphic figurine from 10th century Kuwait depicts a horse formed from earthenware. It was perhaps used as a toy, but it allows us to understand some of the common sights found historically in the Gulf region. Horses as well as other quadrupeds were part of daily life and vital to transportation, commerce, and goods production.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/b6b.contextual_description: Horses and camels were the traditional means of travel for nomadic and semi-nomadic groups in the Hijaz and Levant for generations. While the Hijaz Railway meant to industrialise the pilgrim travel from Damascus to Medina, quadrupeds remained an essential part of the pilgrimage route, as well as vital resources for the construction of the railway itself. Locomotives, iron for the rails, and provisions for the labourers were transported by horses and other hauling animals. While the railway served as a mechanised replacement for their labour, horses and camels remained vital to the path of the railway before, during and after its construction. Importantly, horses also continued to serve as a nationalist image for many Arab countries after the First World War.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/933.contextual_description: The Hijaz Railway and its implications for the transition from quadruped to mechanized travel caused tensions between communities in the region. For example, some Bedouin groups in the Hijaz region opposed the railway project as they made their income partially through protecting and guiding pilgrim camel caravans to Mecca. Their resistance to the railway, sometimes violent, is part of the reason the railway never made it past Medina. Therefore, despite the railroad’s construction, pilgrims still needed to transfer to traditional means of travel like camel caravans to make it to Mecca for Hajj.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/8bc.contextual_description: Although the Hijaz Railway was not completed as planned. The tracks, stations, and associated infrastructures were already finished in many places along the route. The states that inherited these infrastructures thus had to contend with them, either through expansion, reappropriation, or abandonment.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/f2d.contextual_description: This map, written in German, tries to capture multiple overlapping pieces of information about the geography and topography of Medina. The station (Bahnhof) can be seen in the lower left quadrant with the railroad headed north (to Damascus). Reports like this show how interested European powers, such as the German government, could use advisors on infrastructural projects to increase their intelligence building capacity in places previously outside of their reach. German labourers, technicians, and planners obtained exceptional access to Hijazi holy cities previously beyond their view under the pretext of assisting with technological spread.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/1a8.contextual_description: Photos of Medina in 1914 show the large impact the station and railroad had on the urban fabric of the holy city. The Hijaz Railway brought imposing buildings as well as new sensorial experiences such as the roar of the iron on the tracks, the screeching of the breaks as the train pulls into the station, and the pollution produced by the locomotives. After the First World War, the station and the tracks in Medina lost their original purpose as the railway became defunct. Despite this, the presence of the construction remained as an urban fossil of a project with very different intentions.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/899.contextual_description: This image displays photos of locomotives in the areas of Schalchiyah (Shaljiyah) and Margil of Baghdad and Basra respectively. The Berlin-Baghdad Railway was a contemporaneous project to the Hejaz Railway. Similar, however, was the breakdown in the project due to rising international tensions and the eventual outbreak of World War I. Throughout the region, new nations needed to deal with the legacies of late Ottoman infrastructural projects, leading to relics like this “derelict” German locomotive in Baghdad.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/187.contextual_description: This confidential report surveyed the condition of the railways of the Iraqi State Railways and the Trans-Iranian Railway from 1942 and 1944. It covers both the Iraq and Iranian sections of rail, but neither comprehensively. The typewritten text is accompanied by photomechanical prints and detailed technical drawings of locomotives. It includes The Second World War-era British military map showing regional railway networks in the former Ottoman Empire. Manuscript annotations highlight the geopolitical interests of various nations involved in their construction.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/ca1.contextual_description: This confidential report surveyed the condition of the railways of the Iraqi State Railways and the Trans-Iranian Railway from 1942 and 1944. It covers both the Iraq and Iranian sections of rail, but neither comprehensively. The typewritten text is accompanied by photomechanical prints and detailed technical drawings of locomotives. It includes The Second World War-era British military map showing regional railway networks in the former Ottoman Empire. Manuscript annotations highlight the geopolitical interests of various nations involved in their construction.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/776.contextual_description: This confidential report surveyed the condition of the railways of the Iraqi State Railways and the Trans-Iranian Railway from 1942 and 1944. It covers both the Iraq and Iranian sections of rail, but neither comprehensively. The typewritten text is accompanied by photomechanical prints and detailed technical drawings of locomotives. It includes The Second World War-era British military map showing regional railway networks in the former Ottoman Empire. Manuscript annotations highlight the geopolitical interests of various nations involved in their construction.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/0bd.contextual_description: This confidential report surveyed the condition of the railways of the Iraqi State Railways and the Trans-Iranian Railway from 1942 and 1944. It covers both the Iraq and Iranian sections of rail, but neither comprehensively. The typewritten text is accompanied by photomechanical prints and detailed technical drawings of locomotives. It includes The Second World War-era British military map showing regional railway networks in the former Ottoman Empire. Manuscript annotations highlight the geopolitical interests of various nations involved in their construction.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/d76.contextual_description: This 1931 poster advertises travel from London to Baghdad in only eight days by transferring from the Orient Express to the Taurus Express in Istanbul. The train connection from Nusaybin to Baghdad was not completed until 1940, so passengers would have to transfer to a motorcoach for part of the Iraq stretch. The poster prominently displays the ruins of Ctesiphon south of Baghdad, further highlighting that the transportation was more for wealthy European tourists than the original political and religious purpose of the Hijaz Railway.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/e9d.contextual_description: This poster for the Simplon-Orient Express advertises the journey from London to Cairo in seven days. Although the map on the bottom section shows other destinations in Europe and the Middle East, the imagery at the top of the pyramids of Giza foregrounded by lush palm trees centres of a certain geography as the focus of the advertisement. Finally, a small face-less figure of a woman carrying a pot on her head highlights orientalising gaze intrinsic to such advertisements which often feature representations of “native” women.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/35d.contextual_description: The railroad stations and tracks fundamentally altered the built environment in some cities as previously discussed with Medina. While the railroad could help people in crossing large spaces in shorter periods of time, they also required the permanent reallocation of urban space such as here in Damascus. This example of aerial photography of Baramkeh shows how the tracks radiating from the station dominate the urban space to its south.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/a7e.contextual_description: Mohammed Al Saleem’s Fluidity can be used to evoke the landscape experience of travel across the Arabian Peninsula. His work is not a direct reference to the Hijaz Railway, but his abstract treatment of horizon, light, movement, and space can be connected to the visual impressions encountered by travellers moving through desert landscapes. Rather than functioning as a documentary image, the work offers a modern artistic reflection on landscape, distance, and the fluid perception of space in motion. Moving through a space, such as on the fixed track of a railway is both expansive and limiting. One can travel far and fast, but at the expensive of being able to easily travel wide as deviation from the preset track is impossible.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/594.contextual_description: This notice provides the routes and timetables for the Nairn Transportation Company moving mail and some passengers between major urban hubs in the Levant and Mashriq. The advertisement notes that the “Pioners of the Desert” route can securely move mail between Damascus and Baghdad, timed to correspond to the wider imperial infrastructural networks of steamships. The company began its operation in the Middle East after the New Zealander founders served in the British army during World War I. Using decommissioned military vehicles, they returned to the area to pursue commercial interests.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/2de.contextual_description: A column of Australian cavalry gallops along a road on the valley floor into the small town of Shechem in Palestine. The rear of the column is in the foreground, with the front of it just entering the town, whose buildings are visible in the distance. The valley is bordered, to the left and right, by steep-sided hills. Although technologies like trains, automobiles, and buses facilitated supply lines, armed forces still relied on quadrupeds to advance their lines and capture territory.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/ab4.contextual_description: Opened in the early 1960s, the Hurriyah (Liberty) Bridge was a key project in Baghdad’s urban expansion. Its simple beam structure connected the two banks of the Tigris, reflecting the city’s modernist ambitions and the rise of motor traffic. A variety of automobiles share space on the new bridge with pedestrians. The imposition of car culture and the infrastructures to support them further revolutionized urban design, requiring space and investment to allow automobile travel.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/a13.contextual_description: This map of the planned Hijaz Railway from back in 1916 stands reminds us of the large ambition of the original project. Looking at the map with an understanding of what would later happen to the empire, it is astounding to think of a large-scale infrastructural project that crossed so many political and communal borders. After the First World War, infrastructural investments turned to projects that facilitated air and car travel, requiring a massive investment in reconceptualizing urban space.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/f6b.contextual_description: Air France’s advertisement encourages plane travel to North Africa, at the time under French control. We see a sleek airplane hovering above an unspecified North African city where two veiled women walk, and a man looks up towards the sky. The encouragement of tourism to France’s oversees colonies and territories in North Africa was made possible through the expanding technology and infrastructure of plane travel. Similar to the tracks and stations of the Hijaz Railway, the expansion of air travel necessitated the building of airports. However, their size and placement, often outside of major cities, was less overt than the heritage infrastructure of the Hijaz Railway that was often evident in urban areas.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/3fe.contextual_description: This 1930s *Air Orient* poster highlights the French airline’s east–west routes across the Middle East and Asia. It depicts planes simply flying over territory not under the control of the French Empire. Therefore, rather than traveling through other states, French territories around the world were connected in a seamless territory. Produced in a Republican France that was also a vast colonial empire, the poster embodies both the allure of modern aviation and the projection of French influence through new networks of mobility.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/09f.contextual_description: In this note, we see the Italian community of Tunisia sold subscriptions to crowd fund an airplane for their community. Despite Tunisia then being a French territory, the presence of other European communities such as Italians shows that there were multiple interested parties in connecting North Africa to Europe by air. Importantly, the Italian community raised funds for the airplane without direct government support, showing the democratization of air travel for those who could afford it.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/e23.contextual_description: Cities such as Beirut, Damascus, and Baghdad appear alongside Paris and London, connected into a single network of modern mobility. The Art Deco design highlights comfort and speed, projecting air travel as both luxury and imperial reach, where distant places were redrawn as accessible stops on an expanding global map. The picture depicting the interior of the plane also shows the space set aside for luggage, emphasizing the capacity of air travel to facilitate comfortable travel for people to bring large pieces of luggage on their trips or to bring back vast quantities of souvenirs on their travels.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/6db.contextual_description: This 1930s poster for Air Union’s Lignes d’Orient advertises airmail service by hydravion (seaplane), linking Marseille with Naples, Athens, and Beirut. More than speed, it promised a modern rhythm of weekly connections, shrinking distance across the Mediterranean. Designed in striking Art Deco style, the poster reflects how aviation transformed communication and projected France’s presence in the region. An arrow pointing east from Beirut alludes to further commercial expansion.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/fa9.contextual_description: Abdullah Al Muharraqi's Oil Exploration illustrates Bahrain's pioneering role in the Gulf's oil history. Oil was discovered there in 1932, making Bahrain the first Arabian Gulf state to enter the oil era, ahead of Kuwait and Saudi Arabia (1938), Qatar (1939–40), Abu Dhabi (1958), and Oman (1964). Depicting workers around an oil well, the painting frames exploration as a human and social process, not merely a technical one. It illuminates how Bahrain's discovery shifted Gulf societies from pearling and maritime trade toward oil-based modernization, infrastructure, and state formation.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/7b1.contextual_description: Jassim Al Zaini’s piece can be read chronologically from right to left showing the changes in Qatari society due to the discovery of oil in the region. As oil is introduced, traditional commercial and societal practices transition as oil refining allowed for new opportunities for urbanization, industrialization, and commerce. Al Zaini’s depiction of the oil industry, however, is a local one, where Qatari’s negotiate and adapt to the new market domestically, resisting the idea that oil exploitation was purely a foreign-imposed practice.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/cd0.contextual_description: This map shows the water pipes that brought fresh water to the European site of Istanbul. The network of pipes necessitated a close understanding of the typography of the region as well as technological interventions to overcome challenges in such typographies. Water pumping stations facilitated the movement of water eastward, bringing the necessary resource from rural areas to urban consumers.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/bc1.contextual_description: Rutbah Wells, once a desert stop for caravans, became vital to early aviation when aircraft could not yet cover long distances without refuelling. Its wells and facilities made it a lifeline for planes crossing between Amman and Baghdad. Here, technological limits met the desert’s scarcity, turning an ancient caravan halt into a modern hub of mobility.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/82b.contextual_description: This 1950s postcard shows the control tower of Basra Airport with the Iraqi flag flying above. At the time, air travel was celebrated as a symbol of modernization. Expanded in the 1960s with new runways and terminals, the airport connected southern Iraq to regional and international networks. The image reflects how aviation shaped Basra’s urban identity and embodied the country’s modern aspirations.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/413.contextual_description: This photograph by East German photographer Heinz Woost captures a DC-4 aircraft belonging to Lebanon-based Trans-Mediterranean Airways during cargo loading operations. The image reflects both the logistics of mid-20th-century air transport and the United Arab Republic’s pursuit of modernization and international connectivity in the midst of the Cold War.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/f11.contextual_description: Yet another postcard encouraging travel to Syria, printed in the mid-1970s, foregrounds the oil pipelines traversing the country from east to west toward the Mediterranean rather than the routes connecting cities. Set against the backdrop of the global oil crisis, such imagery positioned Syria not only as a tourist destination but also underscored its strategic significance within the geopolitics of energy.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/711.contextual_description: Hamed Owais's *Nasser and the Nationalisation of the Canal* illuminates the Cold War era and the rise of twentieth-century Arab nationalism. Painted in 1957, it depicts Gamal Abdel Nasser's 1956 nationalization of the Suez Canal, a moment emblematic of anti-imperialism and national sovereignty. Owais portrays Nasser as a heroic figure surrounded by the people, transforming political event into collective hope. The work thus reveals how art constructed Nasserist ideology, while also raising questions about the tension between liberation and the centralization of power around charismatic authority.

47693e45-d390-5d8b-b761-f610b3fab532/bf1.contextual_description: Josip Tito and Nasser met in Belgrade to discuss their bilateral relations within the context of the larger Cold War. Charting a third course apart from the standard binary of Cold War geopolitics, Nasser and Jawaharlal Nehru soon after agreed on the premise of the Non-Aligned Movement. The Non-Aligned Movement would later be launch in 1961 from Belgrade, gaining the support of 25 countries around the world.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/571.contextual_description: Here, on a wall in Beirut painted by Yazan Halwani, Fairouz sings for Lebanon, for the Arab world, for anyone who listens. In 1973 she was Warda in the Rahbani brothers' musical Al-Mahatta (The Station), asking after a train on a line that did not exist. The rumour spreads, land prices rise, tickets are sold, and Warda sings Imani Sati', about a belief that does not break and a thing awaited that comes in the end. Then the train really does arrive. Everyone boards, while Warda, who started it all, has no ticket and stays behind. Perhaps all she wanted was a line linking the village to the world. The Hijaz Railway kept that promise for barely a decade. Today much of it survives as its ghost.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/368.contextual_description: Commemoration plays a vital role in collective memory, recalling the past while opening a space for it to be reconsidered and debated. Although the historical landscape has changed profoundly over time, this commemorative coin evokes an ambitious ideal once translated into reality. While its meaning inevitably shifts depending on the viewer's perspective, the coin recalls a moment when steel and stations connected Istanbul to the Hijaz via Damascus, radically easing the arduous journey of Muslim pilgrims and transforming the socioeconomic fabric of the regions it traversed.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/797.contextual_description: Printed in 2008 for the centenary of the Hijaz Railway, these two stamps show a steam engine emerging from a tunnel and another crossing an iron bridge with its black smoke pouring out behind it. A tunnel and a bridge were clear signs of how much nature had to be overcome to reach a destination. They are also a sign of something else, a sovereign state commemorating an achievement from the time when it was a province of the Ottoman Empire. But looked at closely, the map raises a question. Why did the designer choose a map in Spanish?

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/357.contextual_description: This work by Abdullah Hamas, a Palestinian painter, expresses the urban interconnectedness between the holy cities of Jerusalem, Medina, and Mecca. In tying these sacred geographies together along a diagonal axis, Hamas recreates the intwined nature of those holy cities and movement between them as expressed in the original purpose of the Hijaz Railway. The axis, in this sense, reconstitutes a new imagined railway connected centers of urban sacrality in the Hijaz and Levant.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/b3e.contextual_description: The Hajj is one of the five pillars of Islam, but who is able to perform it is determined by quotas and permits. For a Palestinian pilgrim, the quota is only the first obstacle, while the journey itself is the second. This card, issued by the Palestinian Authority, records Khalil al-Nammoura and his wife Fadeyyeh’s application for the 2007 Hajj season (1428 AH). They could travel either by bus or by plane, but in either case their journey began by crossing into Jordan.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/1ad.contextual_description:
The Hajj was not only a spiritual journey but also an administrative and financial undertaking. Registration cards, travel permits and special banknotes issued for pilgrims reveal the complex systems through which pilgrimage was organised, controlled and financed.  
  
Following the partition of British India in 1947, both Pakistan and India introduced special banknotes for pilgrims travelling to Saudi Arabia in the 1950s. Designed to regulate the movement of national currencies abroad, these notes allowed pilgrims to obtain money for their journey while limiting the export of ordinary domestic currency. They were not legal tender in their countries of origin. Indian Hajj notes could be exchanged in Bombay for Indian rupees or pounds sterling. These unusual banknotes show how even a religious journey was shaped by national borders, currency regulations and financial controls.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/33d.contextual_description: Borders and visas limit movement everywhere. For Saudi women, there was an additional barrier until 2019. Women were required to obtain written permission from a male guardian to travel. Manal Al Dowayan collected travel permission documents from Saudi women and girls, ranging in age from six months to sixty years. Among them were scientists, engineers and journalists. She printed their documents onto dove sculptures. The doves hang in the air, suspended as those women once were. Building the means of transport is only part of the story. Who is actually able to travel completes the picture.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/3c3.contextual_description: Being in exile requires an act of travel. Western Asia was no exception to this involuntary movement, and in 1948 hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were forced to leave their homes on foot. Life continued in the camps, in harsh conditions, and people struggled to survive. Artists like Shammout, who had walked that road himself, froze those moments, holding the past and the future in one image. The child sleeps safe in his mother's arms, while her gaze is full of thought for an unknown future elsewhere.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/bdc.contextual_description: When you have to leave your home, you cannot take it with you, only its key. That key holds the memories, the sense of belonging, family and friends, and it holds the hope of return as well. The journey may be by train, by boat, by air or on foot, and the key goes with you. Ahmad Canaan gives that journey a form, a steel boat whose masts are keys. His title asks to what exiled country you are returning, echoing Mahmoud Darwish, who asked those leaving Beirut in 1982 what exile they were returning to.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/635.contextual_description: This Jordanian passport, issued in Amman in November 1979, belonged to Jamal Hasan Ibrahim, a Palestinian who was born in 1936 in Beit Ummar, near al-Khalil (Hebron), and lived in Amman. He worked as a driver, carrying goods across the desert roads between Amman and the Gulf, and within a single year, from November 1979 to November 1980, the pages of his passport filled with visas and stamps from Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. By then it was the roads, not the rails, that connected the peoples of Western Asia.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/56e.contextual_description: Since the 1970s, oil wealth has drawn people from across Asia, Africa and the Arab world to Doha in search of work. With no railway linking the region, many once came overland or by sea. Today almost all arrive by air. Seeking a way to picture Qatar's rapid transformation, Faraj Daham turned to the daily realities of the city. In Street Language, construction workers stand amid yellow and orange heat, their covered faces turned directly towards us. Their oversized feet, a recurring feature of Daham's visual language, seem to bear the weight of the journeys that brought them here.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/448.contextual_description: In Human Landscapes from My Country, written in prison during the Second World War, Nâzım Hikmet uses the train as a stage for people from all walks of life in Turkey. In the locomotive, İsmail the stoker asks Aladdin the engine driver whether the rails go around the whole world. They do, Aladdin says. İsmail presses on: if there were no war and no border controls, could the engine run from one end of the world to the other? The rails stop at the sea, Aladdin replies, then come ships, then planes. In a stoker's question, free travel becomes a promise held back only by war and borders.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/f39.contextual_description: Muzaffar al-Nawwab wrote Li-l-Rayl wa-Hamad (For the Train and Hamad) in the late 1950s, speaking in the voice of a woman aboard a night train heading south from Baghdad. As the train approaches the village where she left her love, Hamad, she urges it to cry out, to slow down at the station, and to pass her village gently. A journey is not only about its destination, but also about the memories the train passes through. The song based on the poem became very popular in Iraq and beyond, reaching many who knew the experience of separation. Today, her image of love as a boat without oars recalls the crossings of the Mediterranean, where separation takes another form.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/a4f.contextual_description: In *A Seat on a Train*, the second section of Mahmoud Darwish’s Four Personal Addresses, the Palestinian poet turns the train into a space of exile and displacement. A collective “we” travels in search of nothing, carrying the keys to a house and a family photograph. Each new station becomes another place of exile. Lanterns, windows and scarves seem to belong to others, while the train carries them onward without bringing them closer to home. Darwish ends it by saying that they cannot become an echo twice, suggesting the impossibility of simply returning to what has been left behind.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/e20.contextual_description: The Arab Train (Ughniyat al-Qitar al-Arabi), a children’s song performed by the Syrian singer and composer Mohammed Diya Al-Din (1932–1978), survives in a black-and-white recording from the archive of Jordanian Television dated 1972. Addressing the driver of an imaginary “Arab train”, the singer asks to be taken to his loved ones in Egypt, Syria and Libya, sends greetings to Kuwait, Qatar, Abu Dhabi and his brothers in Saudi Arabia, several of them newly independent states at the time, wishes to visit Lebanon and his family in Jordan and Iraq, and asks the driver to pass through Sudan and Morocco and stop in Bahrain. With its playful refrain imitating the sound of a train, the song turns the idea of Arab unity into a journey for children, in which borders and distances disappear and the only worry is missing the train. It shows how the railway, long after the Hijaz Railway had ceased to function as a continuous line, lived on in popular culture as an image of connection.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/ccf.contextual_description: “And Then The Birds Flew Over” not only reveals the resilience of nature but also offers a powerful metaphor for the social crises of the Middle East. Soil and water generate new life beyond human-made borders and authoritarian control. This mirrors the struggles of people and ecosystems to endure despite wars, displacement, and political oppression. From a posthuman perspective, the work rejects the idea of absolute human control, reminding us that the region’s destiny is shaped not only by political decisions but also by the resilience of soil, plants, water, and all living beings acting together.

2d07bb0f-b16e-53ad-b710-eb9840a46d50/17c.contextual_description: The telegraph developed in the same era as the railway, but words travelled faster than trains. Then voices followed over the same wires before taking to the air. In July 1953, Sawt al-Arab, the Voice of the Arabs, began broadcasting from Cairo and was soon heard far beyond Egypt. Transistor sets like this one, made by the state company Telemisr, carried it into homes. The same signal served two purposes. It spoke for those in power, and it let those far from home hear a familiar voice, a song, news of a place they had left. This journey needed no rails and no permit.
